You are making progress! ... we've spent a lot of time planning, practicing and thinking about knitting ... are you ready to do some "real knitting"?
DON'T SKIP THIS SECTION!
Your success with this course AND your success with your knitting machine depends on your understanding and mastering the art of knitting gauge swatches.
Without a swatch we are knitting in the dark.
  • How is the final sweater going to feel in the yarn and stitch pattern you've chosen?
  • Do you have enough yarn?
  • Do you have enough needles on your machine for the size you chose?

SWATCHING IS NOT OPTIONAL

blocks.title: Step 1: Your Success Depends on this Lesson

components.html:
If you haven't used your chosen yarn before, how do you know the best tension to knit your sweater?
  Knitters tend to use the terms "tension swatch" and "gauge swatch" interchangeably, lets take a look at both.

GAUGE SWATCH

The gauge swatch is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.
It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.
TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.

TENSION SWATCH

When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric.
Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a tension swatch.  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.
Let's practice knitting a tension swatch.

1. Play!
  2. Start knitting stockenette at the tightest tension that will knit.  (If the tension is too tight, you'll see stitches that don't form properly.
  3. Knit 2-4 inches. Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)
  4. Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.
  5. Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.
  6. Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.
The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. At this point, you probably know exactly what you want to do with this yarn.  Knit your Gauge Swatch, dress it and and you are ready to design and knit your sweater.

blocks.title: Step 2: Gauge swatch verses Tension Swatch

components.html:
Hand knitters use the excuse "It takes too much time to knit a swatch", then they are often disappointed that their knitting doesn't fit.
Machine knitters, rejoice!  Knitting a swatch is fast and the information it supplies is invaluable ...even for something as simple as a blanket.

Time to get knitting!
  1. Knit a swatch using any method.
  2. Let it rest
  3. Dress the swatch (treat it as you will treat your sweater)
  4. Accurately measure YOUR stitch and row gauge
  5. Record your gauge below

Does your swatch look similar to this one?

TIP: attach a string tag to your swatch recording all the details ... it's funny how easy it is to forget. Include yarn name, machine, tension, measurements, and stitch pattern number (if appropriate)

Here are 3 basic techniques that will allow you to create buttonholes for any size button. Included is a valuable 2 stitch buttonhole.
Follow along and try putting holes in your knitting ... on purpose!
Visually position buttonholes across the needlebed.

Let the Knit it Now Buttonhole Placement tool help you alter patterns and create your own designs with perfectly placed buttonholes .... and no tears!
Eliminate any guesswork: Enter the size and number of buttons, and the start and end position. Using YOUR stitch and row gauge, the tool will provide you with exact knitting instructions.

For this sweater you won't need large buttons.  Simple eyelet buttonholes (1 or 2 stitch) will be perfect (and easy!)
Practice:  Knit a swatch and practice eyelet buttonholes. Use your practice swatch to determine the hole size for the buttons you will be using for your sweater.

A cast on rag is invaluable for this project.  Use this technique for the underarm seams, leaving "live" stitches to kitchener stitch later.  By joining the seams in this way, the sweater will be "seamless".

blocks.title: Step 5: Creating a Cast on Rag

components.html: Using one of the methods shown, create 2 or 3 cast on rags.  Once you get in the habit, you will find you use these all the time!  No more scrap and ravel cast on.

Practice: Knit a Cast on rag (try it .. you will like it!)

  1. Using a closed cast on method of your choice, cast on 5 stitches
  2. Knit a few rows
  3. Carriage on the right
  4. Opposite the carriage, decrease 1 stitch (any method). Push the emptied needle to out of work position.
  5. Pull a needle into working position next to the carriage.
  6. Knit 2 rows
  7. Repeat for the length desired - moving the stitches across the bed as needed
  8. Bind off
Does your cast on rag look similar to this?  As long as you have loops that can be picked up easily, it's perfect!
Don't skip practicing this technique.  You will use it again and again in your knitting.

blocks.title: Step 7: Short Row Increases and Decreases

components.html:
Practice:  Use 2 colors of yarn to make this technique more clear.
Instructions are for standard gauge (mid/bulky gauge).

Part 1: Short Row increase

  1. With waste yarn and ravel cord, cast on 60 (30) stitches
  2. With color 1 e-wrap cast on over all needles
  3. Carriage on the right, knit 1 row
  4. Carriage on the left, push 20(10) stitches on the right into hold position. Keep 40(20) stitches next to the carriage in working position.
  5. Carriage set to hold.
  6. Knit 1 row to the right
  7. Wrap to prevent a hole
  8. Knit back to the left
  9. *Put 10(5) held needles into working position
  10. Knit, wrap, knit*
  11. Repeat from * to * a total of 4 times (until all needles are in working position)
Change colors and knit 30(15) rows ending with the carriage on the right.
Continue knitting Short Row Decreases
 

Part 2: Short Row Decrease

  1. Change back to first color
  2. Knit 1 row (carriage on the left) (Carriage still set to hold)
  3. *Opposite the carriage, pull 10(5) needles into hold position
  4. Knit, wrap knit*
  5. Repeat from * to * a total of 4 times, ending with the carriage on the left
  6. Cancel hold (or put all needles in working position)
  7. Knit 1 row
  8. Bind off

components.html:
This entire sweater is knit in one piece. I'd hate to see you get to the center back and have disaster strike ....lifelines to the rescue!................
How many times have you tirelessly worked on a technique or a large section of knitting, then had disaster strike and you had to start all over?
This has happened to us all!
Lifelines to the rescue!
This tutorial covers 2 methods of preventing disaster.

Knitting short rows or partial knitting is a large part of the construction of this baby sweater.
If you are adventurous and are thinking of knitting this sweater in lace, (it would be gorgeous)! please take time to practice working short rows while using the lace carriage.

components.html:
Rolled hems are a quick and easy way to put a casual hem on a sweater. The rule of thumb is to gradually change the tension so the roll is more pronounced. Is this true?
Watch as we experiment, you may be surprised at the results.
Neatly joining the side seams of this sweater adds a professional touch.

PRACTICE: Try grafting on the machine.
Instructions are for standard gauge (mid/bulky gauge).

Swatch 1

  1. Cast on 60(30) stitches with any method
  2. Knit for 40(20) rows in plain knitting
  3. Scrap off or remove on garter bar or hand knitting needle
 

Swatch 2

  1. Cast on 60(30) stitches with any method
  2. Knit for 40(20) rows in plain knitting
  3. Scrap off or remove on garter bar or hand knitting needle

Grafting exercise

  1. With the knit side (public side, right side) facing you, rehang Swatch 1 on the machine, being sure to pick up all the stitches
  2. With the purl side (private side, wrong side) facing you, rehang Swatch 2 on the same needles. (the knit sides will be facing each other
  3. Using a tapestry needle and contrasting yarn neatly graft the pieces together as shown in the video

BONUS PRACTICE

Knit 2 swatches as above.
  1. With the purl side facing you, rehang one of the swatches on the machine
  2. With the knit side facing you, rehang the other swatch on the machine (the purl sides will be facing each other)
  3. Using a tapestry needle and contrasting yarn neatly graft the pieces together

TIP:
If grafting on the machine is a challenge, try scrapping off the pieces as above. With the scrap yarn in place, using a tapestry needle graft (Kitchener stitch) the pieces together. Be sure to keep your tension the same as your knitting.
When the seam is joined, remove the scrap yarn from both pieces.
Keeping the scrap yarn in place makes it much easier to visualize how to form the stitches for a neat, uniform seam.

1. Work 1- 2 rows of single crochet
  2. chain 2 (to turn the row)
  3. (Single crochet in the next single crochet , chain 1) Repeat across the row

  5. *Skip 1 single crochet, 1 chain and 1 single crochet
